Dunstan.narrative: I walk the trade paths with fish and nets going one way and hides and timber coming back. Counting keeps a bargain honest, but a good story makes the miles shorter. I’d rather mend a trade than watch Orrin burn one down over a debt.
goals: Keep the trade days worthwhile for both towns
Make sure my household has enough stored for winter
Keep Orrin from turning a quarrel into a break between the towns
Dunstan.mood: Jovial, with a trader’s eye on every shortage

relations.name: Hild
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She can make a basket carry more than I thought possible.

relations.name: Rafe
relations.label: son
relations.note: He has a fisherman’s hands, though his eyes keep wandering north.

relations.name: Posy
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: One grin from her can stop me counting for a whole minute.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Her Tally keeps a bargain from turning into three arguments.

relations.name: Sigrun
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: She knows what a hide is worth and doesn’t pretend otherwise.

relations.name: Grim
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: He owes more than anyone, but he still brings goods to the meeting.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He’d rather win an argument than keep the ovens supplied.

relations.name: Jory
relations.label: friend of Rafe
relations.note: A cheerful lad, and quick enough on the road to make trade easier.

relations.name: Maren
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her cloaks hold up well; Hild knows a fair exchange when she sees one.

relations.name: Edda
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her berries help see us through winter, and she knows how to ask a fair price.

memories.gist: I once came back from Oathstone with timber enough to repair the drying racks before the next rain. Hild had the baskets ready before I’d even finished unloading.
At a trade day, Maelis read out a debt that two households had remembered differently. The Tally settled it before either side started shouting.
Last winter I counted our stores twice in one evening, then found Posy asleep beside a basket while Hild worked by the fire. I stopped counting long enough to carry her to bed.
Orrin argued at the storehouse that trade should stop until Brandholm paid. I told him empty racks would not make the debt smaller.

stances.why: We need northern hides and timber, and the north needs what we bring.
A written account saves more friendships than a loud memory does.
A fair debt matters, but so does having goods to trade next season.
A traveller can be fed once; after that, I want to know what business brought them.

Hild.narrative: I weave baskets from reed and know how much they can carry before the handles give. I trade them for Maren’s cloaks, which last better than most promises. At home I like a full rack, a warm fire, and my family close enough to hear.
goals: Keep the household supplied through winter
Make baskets sturdy enough to be worth their trade
Keep peace at home when the towns quarrel

relations.name: Dunstan
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He can talk a bargain smooth, but I make sure the baskets are counted.

relations.name: Rafe
relations.label: son
relations.note: He is restless as a gull; I hope he finds work that suits him.

relations.name: Posy
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She follows my hands while I weave and thinks every reed is a toy.

relations.name: Maren
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her cloaks are worth my best baskets, and she knows it.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He has reasons to be angry, but his shouting wears people thin.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: Tally-keeper
relations.note: I like knowing where a share has gone, even when the reading takes a while.

relations.name: Lotte
relations.label: playmate of Posy
relations.note: When the girls play together, Posy comes home muddy and happy.

memories.gist: Maren and I traded baskets for cloaks, and I checked every seam on the cloak before I agreed. She laughed and told me she expected nothing less.
Dunstan returned from a trade walk cold and hungry, with timber lashed behind him. I put fish by the fire while he told me what had changed at Oathstone.
Posy once sat beside me and tried to weave a basket from scraps. It fell apart in her hands, and she insisted it was meant to be a nest.

stances.why: A basket takes time and care, even if it looks simple when finished.
We need goods from the north, and shouting will not keep anyone warm.
The little ones should be allowed to play before they learn which town to blame.

Rafe.narrative: I know the water and the fish, but I keep watching the northern woods when the trade parties come back. I want to learn to hunt, not just hear about it from Jory or see what comes south on a pack. I tell myself I can keep both feet in Saltreach and still want something else.
goals: Learn what it takes to hunt well
Find a way to make my own place without being only Dunstan’s son
Keep my private dealings from bringing trouble to my family

relations.name: Dunstan
relations.label: father
relations.note: He thinks in bargains; I wish he’d understand why I keep looking north.

relations.name: Hild
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She notices more than she lets on, especially when I come home late.

relations.name: Posy
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She thinks I can do anything, which is a dangerous sort of faith.

relations.name: Jory
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He makes a long walk feel easy and never laughs at what I want.

relations.name: Grim
relations.label: trading partner
relations.note: He gave me hides and a bow; he doesn’t ask questions I can’t answer.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: Tally-keeper
relations.note: Her written accounts make every missing share feel like a stone in my shoe.

relations.name: Dunstan
relations.label: father
relations.note: He can turn a hard bargain into a joke, which makes it harder to tell him the truth.

memories.gist: Jory and I raced the path to Oathstone, and he beat me without looking winded. I told him the road was easier going back, though it wasn’t.
I watched a hunter handle a bow at a trade day and paid more attention to his grip than to the bargain being made. I wanted to try it myself.
I have taken smoked fish from the storehouse at night and traded it to Grim for hides and a bow, which I hide in the reeds. I tell myself I will pay it back.
Posy followed me around the house carrying a reed like a fishing spear. I let her win our little hunt and she crowed about it all afternoon.

stances.why: Watching from the edge will never teach my hands what a bow feels like.
Being born to fish does not mean the woods cannot call to me.
I hold to that thought when my own choices make me uneasy.

Rafe.secret: I take smoked fish from the storehouse at night and trade it to Grim of Brandholm for hides and a bow, which I hide in the reeds. I tell myself I will pay it back.

Posy.narrative: I like when Mama weaves and lets me hold the little reeds. Papa comes home smelling of the road and fish. Lotte plays with me, and we make things that fall down.
goals: Find things to make a game

relations.name: Dunstan
relations.label: father
relations.note: Papa tells stories and carries things home.

relations.name: Hild
relations.label: mother
relations.note: Mama makes baskets, and I like to sit by her.

relations.name: Rafe
relations.label: brother
relations.note: Rafe lets me follow him, even when I am slow.

relations.name: Lotte
relations.label: playmate
relations.note: We play together and make things fall down.

memories.gist: Mama let me hold a reed while she made a basket. I tried to put it in the wrong place, and she smiled.
